summary: Defines a stored, file-oriented format for Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data items. It is designed to work well with systems that recognize file types, such as the Unix file command. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers guess what a file is by peeking at its first few bytes. This gives CBOR data a recognizable label at the start so programs know what kind of file it is.

subtitle: Two small tag envelopes that put a recognizable magic number at the start of stored CBOR files.

tldr.problem: Tools like the Unix file command can tell that a file is CBOR at best, but not which CBOR-based format it holds, so stored CBOR files are hard to identify.
tldr.mechanism: A CBOR Protocol gets its own tag, and the file is either wrapped in two nested tags (55799 plus the protocol tag) or begins with a 12-byte label built from tag 55800, the protocol tag and the byte string BOR.
tldr.outcome: Stored files get a deterministic first 8 to 12 bytes that identify the protocol. The RFC also allocates tags for CoAP Content-Formats and a third labeling method for non-CBOR data. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9277 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata for this unit. It is built on CBOR as defined in RFC 8949.

sections.title: The Problem of Identifying Stored Data
sections.content:
Operating systems have long needed to tell which program should handle which file. In Unix, a file is a stream of bytes, so identifying its content is a heuristic job, done for example by the file(1) command. A common technique is a magic number at the start of the file. Other systems rely on file extensions, which are brittle once a file is detached from its type information.

As CBOR is used for more and more artifacts, labelling them as just CBOR is probably not enough. The RFC gives a way to encode a magic number at the start of a CBOR file. Because a format may use a single CBOR data item or a CBOR sequence of items, it presents two enveloping methods, and a CBOR Protocol designer picks one. The RFC was inspired by the disarray of PEM files, which all share the extension pem even when they hold public keys, private keys or certificate requests.
sections.plainLanguage: If every file looks the same from the outside, you cannot tell a photo from a shopping list. A name tag at the very start of each file fixes that.

sections.title: What a Good Magic Number Needs
sections.content:
Ideally a magic number is a fingerprint unique to a specific CBOR Protocol. It sits in the first few bytes of the file (a small multiple of 4), does not change when the contents change, and does not depend on the length of the file.

Less ideal solutions need a pattern in which some bytes must be ignored. The file(1) command can be told to ignore bytes, but this can lead to ambiguities.
sections.plainLanguage: A good name tag is always in the same spot, always says the same thing, and does not change when the file inside changes.

sections.title: The Protocol-Specific Tag
sections.content:
Both methods need a CBOR tag for each kind of object that a CBOR Protocol stores in files. The designer asks IANA for a 4-byte tag, a First Come First Served allocation that needs only a simple request using the template in the CBOR specification. To avoid leading zero bytes, the value must be from 0x01000000 (16777216) to 0xFFFFFFFF (4294967295) inclusive. Values with an embedded zero byte are discouraged because they may confuse code that treats the magic number as a C string.

Four ASCII characters that are mnemonic for the protocol are encouraged but not required. The Openswan example uses OPSN, which gives tag number 1330664270.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of file picks its own four-letter code, such as OPSN, and registers it so nobody else uses the same one.

sections.title: The Two Enveloping Methods
sections.content:
CBOR Tag Wrapped suits protocols that encode a single data item. The item is wrapped in two nested tags: the outer is the self-described CBOR tag 55799, and its content is the protocol-specific tag whose content is the data item. The example for application/senml+cbor, Content-Format ID 112, gives the 8-byte fingerprint d9d9f7da63740171. A protocol may remove the two tags on constrained networks when the type is clear from context.

Labeled CBOR Sequence suits CBOR Sequences (RFC 8742). It prepends a separate 12-byte label item: the outer tag is 55800, the inner tag is the protocol-specific tag, and the content is a 3-byte byte string holding 0x42_4f_52, which is BOR. The ASCII characters CBOR therefore show up in a hexdump. The protocol data follows as the next items, with no further tag, so an application can easily drop the first item.
sections.plainLanguage: One method puts the file in an envelope with two stickers on it. The other staples a small label page in front of a stack of pages.

sections.title: Choosing a Method and the Extra Tag Ranges
sections.content:
Appendix A gives advice. If the on-wire format is new and 8 extra bytes are not a problem, use CBOR Tag Wrapped, so the stored and on-wire formats are identical. If the 8 bytes hurt on the wire, use the Labeled CBOR Sequence for storage. The sequence label is easy to retrofit if programs already read every item in a file. Tag wrapping is easier to retrofit onto an existing single-item format, but a naive program might send the extra tags over the network.

Appendix B and Section 4.3 allocate tag numbers 1668546817 (0x63740101) to 1668612095 (0x6374ffff) for CoAP Content-Format numbers below 65025, using TN(ct) = 0x63740101 + (ct / 255) * 256 + ct % 255, which avoids zero bytes. Appendix D defines a third method, CBOR-Labeled Non-CBOR Data, using tag 55801 in the same 12-byte label, followed directly by the non-CBOR data.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick the envelope if you have one thing to label, and the label page if you have a stack. There is also a way to put a CBOR name tag on files that are not CBOR at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Clearly identifying CBOR contents in files has several effects. The most obvious is that malware can more easily find interesting stored objects and then exfiltrate or corrupt them.

Protective applications cannot rely on the applications they protect to recognize file formats in exactly the same way, which is a check-versus-use issue. End-point assessment tools should not rely only on these labels to decide whether to inspect a file, and the label might change which application is used by default to process the file.
sections.plainLanguage: A clear name tag helps friends and thieves alike, and a guard should not trust the tag alone to decide what to check.
